lines.text: Vegetables are the cornerstone of a healthy diet, providing vitamins, minerals, fibre, and essential nutrients. They can be categorized in several ways. Root vegetables — carrots, potatoes, beetroot, turnips, and sweet potatoes — grow underground and are hearty staples in many cuisines. Leafy greens like spinach, lettuce, kale, and cabbage are nutrient-dense and versatile. Cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli, cauliflower, and Brussels sprouts are known for their health benefits. The allium family — onions, garlic, leeks, and spring onions — forms the flavour base of countless dishes worldwide. Legumes, including peas, beans, and lentils, are excellent sources of protein and fibre. Squash and gourds — courgettes (zucchini), pumpkins, and butternut squash — are popular in soups and roasts. Peppers range from sweet bell peppers to fiery chillies, adding colour and heat to any dish. Tomatoes, cucumbers, and aubergines (eggplants) are botanically fruits but are cooked and eaten as vegetables. Vegetables can be prepared in many ways: raw in salads, steamed, boiled, roasted, grilled, stir-fried, or pickled. Each cooking method brings out different flavours and textures, making vegetables endlessly adaptable.

lines.text: Start with easy ones — tomatoes, courgettes, and lettuce. They grow quickly and don't need much space.

lines.text: What about root vegetables? I love carrots and potatoes.
